I’ve been farming these 50 mu in Quzhou for 30 years, since I was 22. My old man taught me, and now I’ve got my own ways. I finished middle school, so I can read the labels on fertilizer bags and I talk to the seed dealer in town, but mostly I do what’s worked on my own field. Last year my wheat did about 500-odd jin per mu, and the maize did a bit better, around 600 jin. This year I’ll keep the same rotations — winter wheat, summer maize, the whole 50 mu.

For the wheat, I’m planting the same improved variety I’ve used the past three years. I buy it from the dealer in town — it’s not the cheapest, but the kernels are plump and it stands up to the wind better than the old traditional kinds. I’ll rotary-till the field after the autumn corn stalks are chopped. For fertilizer, I put one full bag — that’s 50 jin — of compound fertilizer on each mu as base, that’s the 15-15-15 kind, and then at green-up and jointing I top-dress with urea. I usually do about 40 jin of urea per mu at jointing, and another 20 jin at heading if the weather looks dry. I know that’s maybe a touch more nitrogen than the extension people say, but I’d rather spend the extra 20 yuan per mu on fertilizer than risk a thin ear. Wheat is my main income. I irrigate four times: once after sowing to get it germinated, once before winter if it’s dry, once at jointing, and once at grain-filling. The well water is there, and the electricity cost is nothing compared to losing yield. I spray herbicide right after sowing, then insecticide and fungicide once around flag leaf, and maybe again if I see aphids.

For the summer maize, I plant hybrid seed — Zhengdan or something like it — right after the wheat combine comes through in early June. I don’t deep-plough for maize, no time for that. I either no-till direct seed or do a quick rotary pass if the ground is too hard. I put down 50 jin of compound fertilizer per mu at sowing, and then when the plants are knee-high at big trumpet I spread another 40 jin of urea. That’s my main feeding. I irrigate three times: at sowing if it hasn’t rained, at big trumpet when I fertilize, and at filling if August is hot and dry. Two sprays: herbicide at pre-emergence, and one insecticide-fungicide mix if the armyworms show up, which they usually do.

My neighbors with similar land mostly do the same. I watch them. If everyone is putting an extra half-bag of urea this year because of the high fertilizer prices, I think about it too, but honestly I’d rather stick to what I know. I’ve got 7 mouths at home and some of the kids send money back from working in the city, but the farm still has to pay for itself. I hire a tractor for ploughing and sowing, and I get a few day-laborers for harvest if the family can’t manage it. I expect my wheat to hit around 550 kg per mu if the spring doesn’t dry out, and the maize should give me 650 kg per mu. That’s enough to sell some and keep us fed.
